edges.basis: Exodus promises guarded entry and gradual possession; Numbers commissions representatives to inspect the promised land. Promise does not remove danger, process, or the need to respond to what is seen.
edges.label: Promise of entry and a mission of inspection

edges.basis: Deuteronomy first recalls the command to possess the land and later the people’s proposal to send men. The search proposal follows a command already framed by “do not fear.”
edges.label: Commanded departure and the proposal to search

edges.basis: Numbers locates the camp in Paran immediately before leaders are sent from Paran. The sequence supplies location and timing without making Miriam’s exclusion a stated cause of the mission.
edges.label: From Hazeroth into the mission

edges.basis: Numbers begins with the LORD telling Moses to send; Deuteronomy recalls the people proposing a search that pleased Moses. Neither passage explicitly explains how divine instruction, popular proposal, and Moses’ approval relate in time.
edges.label: Who initiates the mission?

edges.basis: Moses asks for evidence about strength, cities, soil, trees, and fruit; Caleb responds to the resulting report with immediate action. Caleb does not deny the obstacles that the mission was commissioned to observe.
edges.label: Observation and the call to act

edges.basis: The survey records route, inhabitants, fruit, and forty days; the first report presents the land’s fruit and fortified resistance. Shared evidence precedes the later division over what Israel can do.
edges.label: What the men see and what they report together

edges.basis: The men first agree that the land flows with milk and honey, then the ten spread an evil report that it eats its inhabitants. The two descriptions stand in the same report sequence without an explanation of how the ten reconcile them.
edges.label: Fruitful land and land that consumes

edges.basis: Caleb and the ten assess the same land, inhabitants, and fortified cities but reach opposed conclusions about action. Their disagreement concerns ability, threat, and the weight given to the LORD’s promise, not the existence of obstacles.
edges.label: Able to possess or unable to go up

edges.basis: Both witnesses preserve fear, refusal, and desire to reverse the journey. Numbers foregrounds the assembly’s night of weeping and children-as-prey claim; Deuteronomy foregrounds accusation that the LORD hated them and Moses’ remembered answer.
edges.label: The refusal in Numbers and Deuteronomy

edges.basis: Caleb’s later appeal remembers the same danger and his full following decades after he urged Israel to enter. The inheritance fulfills the earlier exception while retaining Anakim, fortified cities, and dependence on the LORD.
edges.label: Caleb’s report and his inheritance

edges.basis: Numbers asks how long Israel will refuse belief after signs; Hebrews concludes that unbelief prevented entry. Hebrews applies the event to new hearers while Numbers preserves the crisis inside its own narrative sequence.
edges.label: Refusal named as unbelief

edges.basis: Moses appeals to the LORD’s proclaimed character, and Nehemiah later remembers God as ready to pardon and sustaining in the wilderness. Nehemiah selects mercy and provision without reproducing the generation sentence in full.
edges.label: Intercession and remembered pardon

edges.basis: Numbers explicitly says the people are pardoned and excluded; Psalm 106 foregrounds unbelief and the raised-hand judgment. Selective memory does not erase Numbers’ coexistence of pardon and sentence.
edges.label: Pardon beside the oath of consequence

edges.basis: Both preserve exclusion of the adult generation, Joshua and Caleb, the children’s entry, and a turn toward the wilderness. Deuteronomy places Moses’ own non-entry beside the sentence; Numbers states it later at Meribah.
edges.label: The generation sentence in Numbers and Deuteronomy

edges.basis: Numbers narrates the plague and the two survivors; Sirach turns that division into memory, warning, and inheritance. Sirach’s moral summary is later reception rather than a replacement for the narrative’s full details.
edges.label: Ten die, two survive, two are remembered

edges.basis: Numbers and Deuteronomy preserve confession, warning, divine absence, presumption, and defeat after the sentence. Numbers names Amalekites and Canaanites; Deuteronomy names Amorites and does not explain the naming difference.
edges.label: The failed ascent in two witnesses

edges.basis: Numbers relates forty spying days to forty wilderness years; Deuteronomy measures thirty-eight years from Kadesh Barnea to Zered. The passages use different endpoints and purposes, but neither supplies a complete arithmetic reconciliation.
edges.label: Forty years and thirty-eight years

edges.basis: Deuteronomy places Moses’ exclusion inside the Kadesh retelling; Numbers states the sentence at Meribah after striking the rock. The texts provide different narrative placements and stated relations without explaining them to one another.
edges.label: Where Moses’ non-entry is located

edges.basis: Moses uses the earlier discouraging report to test whether Reuben and Gad will discourage Israel again. The new land-allotment proposal is compared with the earlier crisis without being declared the same event.
edges.label: A refusal becomes a warning to the next generation

edges.basis: Both missions inspect the land and return with a report about inhabitants and Israel’s prospects. The twelve divide over entry; Joshua’s two hear fear inside Jericho and report that the LORD has delivered the land.
edges.label: Twelve spies and two spies

edges.basis: Numbers records fear for the children; Joshua says those children were raised in place of the refusing generation and brought into the land. The feared outcome is reversed, but the children still live through the cost of wilderness delay.
edges.label: Children feared as prey and raised in their parents’ place

edges.basis: Numbers holds pardon beside exclusion; Ezekiel remembers an oath of non-entry beside God sparing the people from complete destruction. Ezekiel summarizes a wider rebellion field and does not isolate the spies’ report as its only referent.
edges.label: Pardon, preservation, and exclusion

edges.basis: Hebrews quotes Psalm 95 and applies its voice, hardening, wilderness death, and rest warning to a present community. The later argument identifies unbelief while preserving the psalm’s direct appeal to hear today.
edges.label: “Today” and the warning against unbelief

edges.basis: Psalm 95 names the denied outcome as rest; Hebrews argues that Joshua’s entry did not exhaust the promise of rest. The development expands the referent of rest without turning the original land crisis into a merely abstract idea.
edges.label: Land-entry failure and a rest that remains

edges.basis: Hebrews and Jude both turn wilderness unbelief after deliverance into warning for later hearers. Hebrews develops Psalm 95 and rest at length; Jude compresses rescue and later destruction into one reminder.
edges.label: Two later warnings from rescue followed by unbelief

event.centerRule: Numbers 13:1–14:38 remains the Event center. Related texts enter only when they materially prepare, retell, contrast, develop, or remember that Event, and every witness keeps its own wording, agency, sequence, and evidence boundary.

characterAnchors.label: Moses
characterAnchors.note: Sends the tribal leaders, receives their report, falls before the assembly, intercedes, announces the sentence, and later retells the crisis.

characterAnchors.label: Caleb
characterAnchors.note: Quiets the people, urges entry, follows the LORD fully, survives, and later receives Hebron.

characterAnchors.label: Joshua
characterAnchors.note: Is named among the twelve, joins Caleb’s appeal, survives, later sends two spies, and leads the next generation into the land.

characterAnchors.label: The ten spies
characterAnchors.note: Acknowledge the land’s abundance, deny Israel’s ability, spread an evil report, and die by plague.

characterAnchors.label: The assembly
characterAnchors.note: Weeps, complains, fears for its children, proposes return to Egypt, threatens Joshua and Caleb, and receives the sentence.

characterAnchors.label: Aaron
characterAnchors.note: Receives the report with Moses, faces the complaint, and falls before the assembly.

characterAnchors.label: The children
characterAnchors.note: Are feared as prey, wander during the sentence, replace the dead generation, and enter the land.

characterAnchors.label: The LORD
characterAnchors.note: Commands the mission, interprets refusal as unbelief, hears intercession, pardons, sentences, preserves, and later identifies rest.

event.throughline: The trail moves from promise and approach through the twelve-person mission, shared evidence, divided report, national refusal, intercession, pardon and sentence, then follows retelling, delayed entry, inheritance, and later memory.

topic.orientation: Enter the mission in Numbers, inspect where the report divides, and follow refusal, intercession, pardon, sentence, delayed entry, inheritance, and later memory without merging the witnesses.
